title: Family arti

segments.voice: Yesterday, jyoti, the flame: hands passed over it, then to the eyes. Your line was take it.

Evening arti in a childhood home. Dad holding the plate a little too high. A little sister fighting to ring the bell, and ringing it the entire time. An aunt singing half a beat ahead of everyone. The smell of camphor, and dinner waiting in the next room. For ten minutes, the whole house was facing the same way. Years later, what stays often isn't the words. It's who was there. The hour, the flame, the song, the light: all of it works alone. But arti was built for more than one.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE REMEMBER: WHO WAS THERE.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE FACING ONE WAY.` → `TODAY: FAMILY ARTI.`

segments.voice: Look at how arti is put together and you'll see it almost asks for company. It has jobs. Someone holds the lamp. Someone rings the bell, often the youngest, because it's the best job. Everyone sings. Then the plate goes around, and each person takes the light. Even the smallest child has something to do. Hindu tradition names four stages of life, and the second, the householder, grihastha, is the one lived in a home full of people. The Manusmriti calls it the stage that supports the others, the way air supports every living thing, because the householder feeds and gives to all the rest. And the home shrine sits right in the middle of it. Worship isn't something you leave the house to do; the house is where it's done. So evening arti becomes a kind of daily meeting. The day's arguments get paused. The phones go down, or at least face down. For ten minutes, whoever is under that roof stands together before one flame. Real families are complicated, though. Some people live alone. Some live with a partner from another faith, or with none. Nobody is saying anyone has to join; a guest can simply stand in the room, listen and watch. But the invitation matters. Prayer can happen alone, anywhere. Arti done together adds something else: the same small flame passing through every pair of hands under one roof.
screen: `ARTI HAS JOBS: LAMP, BELL, SONG.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER: GRIHASTHA.` · `THE HOUSE IS WHERE IT'S DONE.` · `NO ONE HAS TO. EVERYONE IS ASKED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you could invite to do this with you, even once: a roommate, a parent on a video call, a partner, a child, a friend. Picture them in the room, one of you holding the flame and one ringing the bell, and notice how it feels not to be the only one facing the light. Then think how you might ask them, simply, with no pressure at all; if they say no, that's fine too.
Family arti. Arti done together: one lamp, one bell, one song, and a job for everyone in the house. Today's word.
Your line: one more. No one has to join, and everyone can be asked. That's day one hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In many Hindu homes, evening arti is a family gathering: one person circles the lamp, a child often rings the bell, everyone sings, and the lamp is passed around so each person can take the light.

chat.says: Why does arti need the whole family? Can't you just do it alone?
options: You can, but it's built for company: a job for each person, one shared flame.
No, arti only counts when every single family member takes part in it.
Alone is better, since other people only distract you from the flame.
chat.meaning: Arti works alone, but it has jobs, lamp, bell, song, so even a small child can join. No one has to; anyone can be asked.
